Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.
The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.
The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys.
Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues.
Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.
“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”
The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week.

Apple’s new study looks to improve the effectiveness of AI health tools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
01:26:56 UTC
10:26:56 KST

Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are. The company is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine. Participants will use a new iOS app to ask medical questions and then rate the responses based on criteria including accuracy, detail, and relevance.
Apple’s new study looks to improve the effectiveness of AI health tools
The study will be conducted through a new app where participants can ask health questions and rate the responses.
The app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, with Apple looking for up to 200,000 people to contribute. Participants 21 and older must be based in the US, and although the app doesn’t use Apple Intelligence, it does require an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 26 or later.
Study participants can use the app to ask health-related questions and receive easily understandable responses with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources. The app relies on text-based prompts, and while dictation is an option using the iOS keyboard, the app isn’t integrated with Siri or Apple Intelligence.
During enrolment, participants are given the option to share Apple HealthKit data, like their activity, sleep, or clinical lab results, so responses will include more context about their own personal health. But privacy is a priority, and Apple says it has taken measures to ensure users’ information remains confidential and the data collected won’t be used to train AI models. The aim is to improve the design and functionality of AI-powered health tools so they can deliver relevant health information that’s easier for users to understand and act on.
“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life. Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” said Sumbul Desai, MD, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness.

FAA Router In Middle-of-nowhere Arkansas Identified as Cause of Nationwide Flight Chaos (nypost.com) 55
			
		 	
				Though the nationwide flight-grounding ended Friday, "Nearly 2,300 flights in the U.S. have been cancelled Sunday in the aftermath..." reports ABC News.    "Additionally, some 18,689 flights were delayed, per FlightAware."
But "a single malfunctioning FAA router in rural Arkansas appears to have caused the air travel chaos,"
reports the New York Post:
The problem originated at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a newly installed router flooded the network with excessive data traffic, disrupting communications between pilots and air traffic controllers, the Wall Street Journal reported. "We saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate, a thousand connections over every four to five seconds," Rebecca Guy, the FAA's technology chief, said on Saturday. ..   [U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean] Duffy said the failure occurred during routine maintenance to replace aging copper telecommunications with fiber-optic cables — part of a broader effort to modernize the FAA's outdated infrastructure.  The router began flooding other devices across the air traffic control network with connection attempts, disrupting both communications with aircraft and radar feeds.  A radar station in Amarillo, in the Texas panhandle, is also being eyed as contributing to the outage.   
And new flight cancellations reported for Monday already stood at 144 as of Sunday afternoon, with 641 delayed, reports ABC News (citing data from Flight Aware):
A spokesperson for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, the company that manufactured the routers believed to be central to the ground stop, said in a statement to ABC News that the devices were working properly Friday, when the ground stop occurred. "Based on what we know today, the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer. It did not fail or act improperly," the statement said...
L3 Harris is a government contractor that provides technology and IT support for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and that worked with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Juniper to install the routers.  "We have that router in the L3 Harris lab down in Florida," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told co-anchor Martha Raddatz on ABC's "This Week" Sunday, referring to the specific router in Arkansas that officials believe caused instability in the air traffic communication system Friday afternoon.  
"L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday.

Skydio's asymmetrical F10 Lightrunner solves a problem with fixed-wing drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
00:03:12 UTC
09:03:12 KST

Skydio’s drones have always been magical. From MIT research and early prototypes to what I would argue is still the most advanced consumer drone ever made, this is a company that makes very cool stuff. Sadly, Skydio no longer makes cool stuff for consumers, instead focusing on drone platforms for public safety, inspection, and other things that, on a good day, don’t affect me personally.
Even so, a new drone from Skydio is worth paying attention to, especially when it’s as weird as this one—the F10 Lightrunner is a fixed-wing camera drone designed for autonomous deployment and high-speed flight, all while looking so lopsided that it’s surprising that it can actually fly.
The benefits of asymmetrical aircraft
There’s a short rabbit hole you can go down if you start looking for other examples of asymmetrical aircraft. In the 1990s, legendary aircraft designer Burt Rutan and his company Scaled Composites built some decidedly odd airplanes, including the Model 202 Boomerang. But perhaps the most famous asymmetrical aircraft was the Blohm & Voss BV 141, a World War II-era reconnaissance plane that featured an engine in the middle alongside a crew compartment alarmingly offset out onto the right wing. The unique design was intended to give the crew the best possible view for reconnaissance missions, because in a typical single-engine aircraft, the crew sits right behind the engine, limiting forward visibility.
Nearly 90 years later, the Skydio F10 is applying a similar philosophy to fixed-wing reconnaissance drones, which typically track targets by flying around them in circles. “While turning at low altitudes, it becomes very hard to avoid occluding a camera with a wing or a tail,” explains Andrew Goessling, director of engineering at Skydio. “So we were analyzing a lot of these use cases, and one of our engineers just blurted out, ‘What if we put the camera on the wingtip?’ And that’s where it all started, because as long as you only turn left, a lot of these problems just go away.”
Of course, putting the camera on the F10’s wingtip creates a bunch of new problems, chief among them that the aircraft is no longer balanced. Not only is the camera payload fairly heavy relative to the total mass of the drone, but its bulk also creates greater drag. This is why the seemingly straightforward solution of putting something else (like a battery) on the other wingtip to rebalance the drone isn’t practical, says Goessling. “The issue there is that the camera represents a substantial portion of the total aircraft drag, so putting something else on the other wing would cut your flight time nearly in half.”
The F10’s wing-mounted camera payload necessitated asymmetrical wings and uneven motor placement.Skydio
Goessling points out that there’s nothing inherently bad about an asymmetric design like the F10; it just makes the life of engineers either a little more difficult or a little more exciting, depending on your perspective. “There were really two challenges here: What is the optimal design for an aircraft with a wingtip camera, and then once you have the design, how are you going to control it?”
Any fixed-wing aircraft design has to consider three factors: distribution of mass, how thrust is distributed between the motors, and how the shape and location of the wings affect the aircraft’s aerodynamics. Once Skydio decided on their requirements for the F10—including the wingtip camera, two motors to enable controllable hovering for takeoff and landing, and a high top speed and long flight time—the engineers used a modeling-and-optimization approach to explore design options. The resulting aircraft compensates for the wing-mounted camera payload by extending just that wing to provide more lift on that side, and repositioning the motors asymmetrically to balance thrust against the added drag of the camera.
Maneuvering with MegaDock
The MegaDock can autonomously launch, recover, and recharge up to five F10 drones using a robot arm to grab them out of the air.Skydio
An added challenge was getting the F10 to launch and recover with a robot arm, using a storage, charging, and deployment system called the MegaDock. That requires the drone to transition from hover to forward flight and then back again—a particularly difficult trick for a flying wing with no tail control surfaces (movable parts of the wing used to steer the aircraft). The F10 uses model predictive control (a control technique based on a detailed physics model of the robot) to accomplish this autonomously, and a single control policy can handle the robot all the way through its entire flight envelope, from a stationary hover to its maximum flight speed of 100 miles per hour. In other words, there’s no “hover mode” or “flight mode,” so the mission planner just tells the drone where it needs to be, and the drone will know how to get itself there.
In operation, Skydio’s MegaDock can handle up to five F10s, allowing for continuous flight operations with three drones while two recharge. The entire system is fully autonomous, with humans only needed for remote supervisory control, communicating with the F10 via dual 5G cellular modems. Maximum flight time is 2 hours, and the aircraft is equipped with the same kind of magical obstacle-dodging camera setup as Skydio’s quadrotor drones. If something goes seriously wrong, an integrated parachute in the F10’s butt will deploy, lowering the drone to the ground gently enough to safely fly over people.
Goessling is the first to acknowledge that the F10 Lightrunner is an unconventional design, but he’s proud of what he and his team have come up with as a commercially viable solution to the occlusion issue with other fixed-wing drones. “It looks weird, and we got some pushback from some of the less technical parts of the company,” Goessling says. “If there were less crazy ways of doing it, we would have pursued them. But we have the data. We have sound reasons for every decision we’ve made. And the outcome at the end was well worth it.”

- Skydio Demonstrates Incredible Obstacle-Dodging Full Autonomy With New R1 Consumer Drone ›
- Skydio 2 Review: This Is the Drone You Want to Fly ›
Evan Ackerman is a senior editor at IEEE Spectrum. Since 2007, he has written over 6,000 articles on robotics and technology. He has a degree in Martian geology and is excellent at playing bagpipes.

What's Next for Nvidia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-15
23:55:55 UTC
08:55:55 KST

Nvidia’s board announced that Jensen Huang had resigned 33 years after he co-founded the company.
What happens to a company when a visionary CEO is gone? Most often innovation dies and the company coasts for years on momentum and its brand. Rarely does it regain its former glory.
That’s the danger facing Nvidia. Here’s what their board should be considering.
Here’s why.
Jensen Huang reinvented Nvidia three times. In 2006 he launched CUDA, turning a graphics chip for PC gamers into a general-purpose computing platform – and funded it for years ahead of any revenue. In 2012, when researchers used Nvidia chips to win the ImageNet contest, he pointed the company to deep learning. In 2020, with the acquisition of Mellanox, Nvidia went from selling boards with GPUs to selling integrated racks that power AI datacenters.
These were not just product transitions, but radical business model transitions; new channels, new customers and new markets. Nvidia pivoted from a vendor of graphics boards, to a software platform, and then to systems company. It’s hard to imagine a CEO focused on executing an existing business model funding CUDA through those years.
Steve Jobs did the same at Apple, transforming it from a niche computer company into the most profitable company in the world. Between 2001 and 2008, Jobs reinvented the company three times.
Visionary CEOs are not “just” great at assuring world-class execution of a successful business model, they are also world-class innovators.
The best are agile and know how to pivot, making substantive changes to their business model while or before their market has shifted. The very best of them shape markets – they know how to create new markets by seeing opportunities before anyone else. They remain entrepreneurs.
Visionary CEOs don’t need someone else to demo the company’s key products for them. They deeply understand products, and they have their own coherent and consistent vision of where the industry/business models and customers are today, and where they need to take the company. They know who their customers are because they spend time talking to them. They use strategy committees and the exec staff for advice, but none of these CEOs pivot by committee.
Microsoft and Apple are two examples of what happens when a visionary CEO is replaced by an execution CEO.
Microsoft and the Cost of Missing the Next Market
Microsoft entered the 21st century as the dominant software provider for anyone who interacted with a computing device. After running Microsoft for 25 years, Bill Gates handed the reins of Microsoft to Steve Ballmer in January 2000. Ballmer went on to run Microsoft for the next 14 years. 
Ballmer organized the company around execution of its then current strengths – Windows and Office businesses. He tripled Microsoft’s sales to $78 billion and profits more than doubled from $9 billion to $22 billion, but those results hid missed opportunities that would reshape computing.
Ballmer failed to understand and execute on the five most important technology trends of the 21st century: in search – losing to Google; in smartphones – losing to Apple; in mobile operating systems – losing to Google/Apple; in media – losing to Apple/Netflix; and in the cloud – losing to Amazon.
In early 2014, Satya Nadella took charge. Nadella got Microsoft organized around the cloud (Azure), freed the Office and Azure teams from Windows and killed the phone business. Nadella saved Microsoft from irrelevance. Today Microsoft is worth about $4 trillion. It is one of the few companies that regained its former glory, after its board replaced a salesman with a product and engineering insider.
Innovation CEOs Hire Execution VPs
Successful visionary CEOs build an executive staff of world-class operating executives and technical leaders (and they unconsciously force out any world-class innovators from their direct reports). The problem is in a company driven by a visionary CEO; there is only one visionary.
Nvidia is the extreme case. Jensen had about 60 direct reports and discouraged one-on-one meetings. No long-term plans. Much like Jobs, he made himself the point where technical, product and business decisions came together. Replacing that role is harder than filling a box on an organization chart. He said he didn’t believe in succession planning.
When visionary founders depart (resignation, death, firing, etc.), their operating executives believe it’s their turn to run the company. At Microsoft, Bill Gates chose Steve Ballmer, and at Apple Steve Jobs chose Tim Cook. Jensen anointed no one.
Once in charge, one of the first things these operations/execution CEOs do is to get rid of the chaos and turbulence in the organization. Execution CEOs value stability, process and repeatable execution. On one hand that’s great for predictability, but it often starts a creative death spiral – creative people start to leave, and other executors (without the innovation talent of the old leader) are put into more senior roles – hiring more process people, which in turn forces out the remaining creative talent. This culture shift ripples down from the top and what once felt like a company on a mission to change the world now feels like another job.
(Amazon is a counterexample. Before succeeding Jeff Bezos, Andy Jassy had already founded and led AWS. He was an innovator who had built a new business inside the existing company.)
At Nvidia this step isn’t optional. No one else can run a company with 60 direct reports, so the next CEO’s first move will be to add layers of management.
Why Tim Cook Was the New Steve Ballmer
Tim Cook ran Apple for 15 years. Apple under Cook grew its revenues from $108 billion to $416 billion and its market value from $350 billion to about $4 trillion. The iPhone continued its annual upgrades of incremental improvements. The transition to Apple silicon showed that major technical change on the chip level was possible under his leadership. But Apple silicon was a better engine for the existing products Apple already had, not a new market.
Apple stumbled badly on the one major product category launched under Cook – Apple Vision Pro and missed badly on AI (Siri was actually first with a Chatbot.) This year it turned to Google to help fix Siri. In September 2026 Cook handed the job to John Ternus.
How Nvidia Could Miss the Boat
The threat to Nvidia is already visible: its biggest customers are becoming its competitors. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Tesla are all building their own AI chips. Jensen’s answer was to keep innovating and bring to market a new generation of chips every year, build a moat around an integrated hardware and software platform (CUDA), and invest ~$50 billion in the AI labs that run on Nvidia. 
It’s likely these are the bets an execution CEO trims first.
The irony is that in the 21st century, the tighter you hold on to your current product/markets, the likelier you will be disrupted. The rapid change of technology will create new disruptions that will force “bet the company” decisions about product direction, markets, pricing, supply chain, operations and the reorganization necessary to execute a new business model. In the GPU market, the difference between market dominance and Chapter 11 may be a hands-on product/customer, and business model-centric CEO with an entrepreneurial vision of the future.
Four Challenges for the Board of Directors
The dilemma facing the board at Nvidia or any board of directors on the departure of an innovative CEO is strategic: Do we still want to be an innovative, risk taking company? Or should we now focus on execution of our core business, reduce our risky bets and maximize shareholder return. Ultimately a board would like both – preserving the speed and ambition of Jensen’s decision-making while distributing enough authority for the company to function without him.
Tactically, that question results in asking: Do you search for another innovator from outside, promote one of the executors or go deeper down the organization to find an innovator?
Herein lies four challenges.
-  Steve Jobs and Bill Gates chose execution executives as their successors. The result was they confused world-class execution with the passion for product and customers, and market insight. From the perspective of Gates there was no difference between him and Ballmer and Jobs believed Cook could be equally creative. Yet history has shown they were world-class stewards of a business model each had been handed. Yet long-term survival in markets that change rapidly require innovation and execution.. 
Nvidia’s board has a different version of this problem. Jensen suggested no one, and he left the board the day he left the job. The decision belongs to a board in crisis, led by the first chair the company has ever had. Boards in crisis reach for stability. That gets you an execution CEO by a different road. Nvidia’s board should ask what its candidates have built under uncertainty.
- If the board decides that the company needs another innovator at the helm, you can almost guarantee that the best executor – the number 2 and/or 3 vice president in the company – will leave, feeling that they deserved the job. Now the board is faced with not only having lost its CEO, but potentially the best of the executive staff.
-    Many innovative/visionary CEOs have become part of the company’s brand. Steve Jobs, Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and Jensen Huang. This isn’t a new phenomenon, think of 20th-century icons like Walt Disney, Edwin Land at Polaroid and Henry Ford. But they’re not only an external face to the company, they were often the touchstone for internal decision-making. Years after a visionary CEO is gone, companies are still asking, “What would Walt Disney/Steve Jobs/Henry Ford have done?” rather than figuring out what they should now be doing in the changing market.
Jensen was more than the brand. He set Nvidia’s foreign policy, and was the company’s face in Washington, Beijing and Taipei. No Nvidia operating VP has done that job. The next Nvidia CEO inherits a Congress and investigators asking how many restricted Nvidia chips reached China.
- As companies grow larger and management falls prey to the fallacy that it only exists to maximize shareholder short-term return on investment, companies become risk averse. Large companies and their boards live in fear of losing what they spent years gaining (customers, market share, revenue, profits.) This may work in stable markets and technologies. But today very few of those remain. And certainly not Nvidia’s market.
Lessons Learned
-  Nvidia’s order book and CUDA will make the next two or three years look fine no matter who is CEO 
  - (unless a meaningful share of that revenue turns out to be chips that were diverted to China.)
- Innovation CEOs are almost always replaced by one of their execution VPs
  - If they have inherited a powerful business model (like Nvidia) this often results in gains in revenue and profits that can continue for years
  - However, as soon as the market, business model, technology shifts, these execution CEOs are ill-equipped to deal with the change
  - The result is a company obsoleted by more agile competitors and their company is left to live off momentum in its twilight years
- Nvidia’s board has to decide what it is hiring its next CEO to do. Executing today’s business is essential. So is reinventing it before someone else makes it obsolete.
- Execution pays your salary, innovation pays your pension
Filed under: National Security |

What's Next for Nvidia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-15

Nvidia’s board announced that Jensen Huang had resigned 33 years after he co-founded the company.
What happens to a company when a visionary CEO is gone? Most often innovation dies and the company coasts for years on momentum and its brand. Rarely does it regain its former glory.
That’s the danger facing Nvidia. Here’s what their board should be considering.
Here’s why.
Jensen Huang reinvented Nvidia three times. In 2006 he launched CUDA, turning a graphics chip for PC gamers into a general-purpose computing platform – and funded it for years ahead of any revenue. In 2012, when researchers used Nvidia chips to win the ImageNet contest, he pointed the company to deep learning. In 2020, with the acquisition of Mellanox, Nvidia went from selling boards with GPUs to selling integrated racks that power AI datacenters.
These were not just product transitions, but radical business model transitions; new channels, new customers and new markets. Nvidia pivoted from a vendor of graphics boards, to a software platform, and then to systems company. It’s hard to imagine a CEO focused on executing an existing business model funding CUDA through those years.

Mini.nvim Is Now on Tangled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-15
23:55:41 UTC
08:55:41 KST

- Lua 100%
- Shell <1%
- Makefile <1%
- Scheme <1%
- Vim Script <1%
All-in-one plugin #
Library of 45+ independent Lua modules improving overall Neovim (version 0.10 and higher) experience with minimal effort. They all share same configuration approaches and general design principles.
Think about this project as "Swiss Army knife" among Neovim plugins: it has many different independent tools (modules) suitable for most common tasks. Each module can be used separately without any startup and usage overhead.
If you want to help this project grow but don't know where to start:
- Leave a star for 'mini.nvim' (on any supported code forge) and/or any other MINI projects.
- Check out contributing guides.
See change log for a history of changes, including current development version.
See MiniMax for a full config example based on 'mini.nvim'.
Note
This was previously hosted at echasnovski/mini.nvim. It was transferred to a dedicated organization to improve long term project stability. See more details here.
Table of contents #
Installation #
This project is hosted on several code forges (use preferred link in the installation code snippet):
- https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim (main)
- https://tangled.org/nvim-mini.org/mini.nvim (mirror)
- https://codeberg.org/nvim-mini/mini.nvim (mirror)
There are two branches to install from:
- main (default, recommended) will have latest development version of plugin. All changes since last stable release should be perceived as being in beta testing phase (meaning they already passed alpha-testing and are moderately settled).
- stable will be updated only upon releases with code tested during public beta-testing phase in main branch.
Here are code snippets for some common installation methods:
- (Recommended) With vim.pack (on Neovim 0.12 and newer): 
  - Main branch: vim.pack.add({ 'https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim' })
  - Stable branch: vim.pack.add({
  { src = 'https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim', version = 'stable' },
})
- Manually with git clone (compatible with mini.deps):
-- Put this at the top of 'init.lua'
local path_package = vim.fn.stdpath('data') .. '/site'
local mini_path = path_package .. '/pack/deps/start/mini.nvim'
if not vim.uv.fs_stat(mini_path) then
  vim.cmd('echo "Installing `mini.nvim`" | redraw')
  local clone_cmd = {
    'git', 'clone', '--filter=blob:none',
    -- Uncomment next line to use 'stable' branch
    -- '--branch', 'stable',
    'https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim', mini_path
  }
  vim.fn.system(clone_cmd)
  vim.cmd('packadd mini.nvim | helptags ALL')
  vim.cmd('echo "Installed `mini.nvim`" | redraw')
end
- With folke/lazy.nvim: 
  - Main branch: { 'nvim-mini/mini.nvim', version = false },
  - Stable branch: { 'nvim-mini/mini.nvim', version = '*' },
- Every module is also distributed as a standalone Git repository. Check out module's information for more details.
Important: don't forget to call module's setup() (if required) to enable its functionality.
Note: if you are on Windows, there might be problems with too long file paths (like error: unable to create file <some file name>: Filename too long). Try doing one of the following:
- Enable corresponding git global config value: git config --system core.longpaths true. Then try to reinstall.
- Install plugin in other place with shorter path.
Modules #
'mini.nvim' contains many modules which is slightly daunting at first. All of them can be used independently, one at a time.
For easier exploration, here they are presented in groups based on module's primary functionality (although some modules can fit in several groups). See more detailed listing here.
Text editing #
These modules improve your text editing experience. Start with 'mini.ai', 'mini.operators', and 'mini.surround'.
General workflow #
These modules improve your general workflow. Start with 'mini.bracketed', 'mini.files', and 'mini.pick'.
Appearance #
These modules improve your Neovim appearance. Start with 'mini.hues', 'mini.icons', and 'mini.statusline'.
Other #
These modules don't quite fit in any of the previous categories.
General principles #
Design #
Each module is designed to solve a particular problem targeting balance between feature-richness (handling as many edge-cases as possible) and simplicity of implementation/support. Granted, not all of them ended up with the same balance, but it is the goal nevertheless.
Independence #
Modules are independent of each other and can be run without external dependencies. Although some of them may need dependencies for full experience.
Structure #
Each module is a submodule for a placeholder "mini" module. So, for example, "surround" module should be referred to as "mini.surround". As later will be explained, this plugin can also be referred to as "MiniSurround".
Setup #
- Each module you want to use should be enabled separately with require(<name of module>).setup({}). Possibly replace {} with your config table or omit altogether to use defaults. You can supply only parts of config, the rest will be inferred from defaults.
- Call to module's setup() always creates a global Lua object with coherent camel-case name: require('mini.surround').setup() creates _G.MiniSurround. This allows for a simpler usage of plugin functionality: instead of require('mini.surround') use MiniSurround (or manually :lua MiniSurround.* in command line); available from v:lua like v:lua.MiniSurround. Considering this, "module" and "Lua object" names can be used interchangeably: 'mini.surround' and 'MiniSurround' will mean the same thing.
- Each supplied config table is stored in config field of global object. Like MiniSurround.config.
- Values of config which affect runtime activity can be changed on the fly to have effect. For example, MiniSurround.config.n_lines can be changed during runtime; but changing MiniSurround.config.mappings won't have any effect (as mappings are created once during setup()).
- If module works best with some specific non-default option value, it is set during setup(). If the value is not essential to module's functionality, it is done only if user or another plugin hasn't set it beforehand (no matter the value).
Buffer local configuration #
Each module can be additionally configured to use certain runtime config settings locally to buffer. See mini.nvim-buffer-local-config section in help file for more information.
Buffer names #
All module-related buffers are named according to the following format: mini<module-name>://<buffer-number>/<useful-info> (forward slashes are used on any platform; <useful-info> may be empty). This structure allows creating identifiable, reasonably unique, and useful buffer names. For example, 'mini.files' buffers are created per displayed directory/file with names like minifiles://10/path/to/displayed/directory.
Disabling #
Each module's core functionality can be disabled globally or locally to buffer. See "Disabling" section in module's help page for more details. See mini.nvim-disabling-recipes section in main help file for common recipes.
Silencing #
Each module providing non-error feedback (like a reminder to press a key after some idle time in 'mini.ai', 'mini.jump2d', 'mini.surround') can be configured to not do that by setting config.silent = true (either inside setup() call or on the fly).
Highlighting #
Appearance of module's output is controlled by certain set of highlight groups (see :h highlight-groups). By default they usually link to some semantically close built-in highlight group and are ensured to be defined after any color scheme takes effect. Use :highlight command or vim.api.nvim_set_hl() Lua function to customize highlighting. To see a more calibrated look, use 'mini.hues', 'mini.base16', or plugin's color scheme.
Stability #
Each module upon release is considered to be relatively stable: both in terms of setup and functionality. Any non-bugfix backward-incompatible change will be released gradually as much as possible.
Not filetype and language specific #
Including functionality which needs several filetype/language specific implementations is an explicit no-goal of this project. This is mostly due to the potential increase in maintenance to keep implementation up to date. However, any part which might need filetype/language specific tuning should be designed to allow it by letting user set proper buffer options and/or local configuration.
Text edit repeat #
All text edit mappings (like for operators, textobjects, motions) created by modules support built-in repeat functionality if technically possible. This includes dot-repeat, macros, and Neovim>=0.13 multicursor.
Plugin color schemes #
This plugin comes with several color schemes (all have both dark and light variants). Activate any of them as a regular colorscheme (like :colorscheme minischeme or vim.cmd.colorscheme('minischeme')).
- Based on 'mini.hues' (recommended): 
  - minischeme: blue and yellow main color scheme.
  - miniwinter: "icy winter" palette with azure background.
  - minispring: "blooming spring" palette with green background.
  - minisummer: "hot summer" palette with brown/yellow background.
  - miniautumn: "cooling autumn" palette with purple background.
  - randomhue: random background and foreground of the same hue with medium saturation.
You can see how they look in 'mini.hues' README.
- Based on 'mini.base16': 
  - minicyan: cyan and grey main colors with medium contrast and saturation palette.
  - miniblue: blue and yellow main colors with high contrast and saturation palette.
You can see how they look in 'mini.base16' README.
Planned modules #
This is the list of modules I currently intend to implement eventually (as my free time and dedication will allow), in alphabetical order:
- 'mini.abbrev' - helper to manage/setup Insert mode abbreviations.
- 'mini.cycle' - cycle through alternatives with pre-defined rules. Something like monaqa/dial.nvim and AndrewRadev/switch.vim
- 'mini.folds' - more capable and user-friendly folds.
- 'mini.repl' - extendable wrapper for REPLs with built-in support for R, Python, Julia, and maybe (just maybe) some AI tools.
- 'mini.sendtext' - send text between buffers. In particular between regular and built-in terminal buffers.
- 'mini.terminals' - coherently manage interactive terminal buffers. Something like kassio/neoterm. Might also incorporate functionality to asynchronously run code in shell with post-processed results.
- 'mini.quickfix' - more capable and user-friendly quickfix list. Possibly with preview and inline editing for search-and-replace workflow.
- 'mini.windows' - window manager. Interactive picker, layout organizer, and maybe more.

- https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim (main)
- https://tangled.org/nvim-mini.org/mini.nvim (mirror)
- https://codeberg.org/nvim-mini/mini.nvim (mirror)
There are two branches to install from:
- main (default, recommended) will have latest development version of plugin. All changes since last stable release should be perceived as being in beta testing phase (meaning they already passed alpha-testing and are moderately settled).
- stable will be updated only upon releases with code tested during public beta-testing phase in main branch.
Here are code snippets for some common installation methods:
- (Recommended) With vim.pack (on Neovim 0.12 and newer): 
  - Main branch: vim.pack.add({ 'https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim' })
  - Stable branch: vim.pack.add({
  { src = 'https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim', version = 'stable' },
})
- Manually with git clone (compatible with mini.deps):
-- Put this at the top of 'init.lua'
local path_package = vim.fn.stdpath('data') .. '/site'
local mini_path = path_package .. '/pack/deps/start/mini.nvim'
if not vim.uv.fs_stat(mini_path) then
  vim.cmd('echo "Installing `mini.nvim`" | redraw')
  local clone_cmd = {
    'git', 'clone', '--filter=blob:none',
    -- Uncomment next line to use 'stable' branch
    -- '--branch', 'stable',
    'https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim', mini_path
  }
  vim.fn.system(clone_cmd)
  vim.cmd('packadd mini.nvim | helptags ALL')
  vim.cmd('echo "Installed `mini.nvim`" | redraw')
end
- With folke/lazy.nvim: 
  - Main branch: { 'nvim-mini/mini.nvim', version = false },
  - Stable branch: { 'nvim-mini/mini.nvim', version = '*' },
- Every module is also distributed as a standalone Git repository. Check out module's information for more details.
Important: don't forget to call module's setup() (if required) to enable its functionality.
Note: if you are on Windows, there might be problems with too long file paths (like error: unable to create file <some file name>: Filename too long). Try doing one of the following:
- Enable corresponding git global config value: git config --system core.longpaths true. Then try to reinstall.
- Install plugin in other place with shorter path.
Modules #
'mini.nvim' contains many modules which is slightly daunting at first. All of them can be used independently, one at a time.
For easier exploration, here they are presented in groups based on module's primary functionality (although some modules can fit in several groups). See more detailed listing here.
Text editing #
These modules improve your text editing experience. Start with 'mini.ai', 'mini.operators', and 'mini.surround'.
General workflow #
These modules improve your general workflow. Start with 'mini.bracketed', 'mini.files', and 'mini.pick'.
Appearance #
These modules improve your Neovim appearance. Start with 'mini.hues', 'mini.icons', and 'mini.statusline'.
Other #
These modules don't quite fit in any of the previous categories.
General principles #
Design #
Each module is designed to solve a particular problem targeting balance between feature-richness (handling as many edge-cases as possible) and simplicity of implementation/support. Granted, not all of them ended up with the same balance, but it is the goal nevertheless.
Independence #
Modules are independent of each other and can be run without external dependencies. Although some of them may need dependencies for full experience.
Structure #
Each module is a submodule for a placeholder "mini" module. So, for example, "surround" module should be referred to as "mini.surround". As later will be explained, this plugin can also be referred to as "MiniSurround".
Setup #
- Each module you want to use should be enabled separately with require(<name of module>).setup({}). Possibly replace {} with your config table or omit altogether to use defaults. You can supply only parts of config, the rest will be inferred from defaults.
- Call to module's setup() always creates a global Lua object with coherent camel-case name: require('mini.surround').setup() creates _G.MiniSurround. This allows for a simpler usage of plugin functionality: instead of require('mini.surround') use MiniSurround (or manually :lua MiniSurround.* in command line); available from v:lua like v:lua.MiniSurround. Considering this, "module" and "Lua object" names can be used interchangeably: 'mini.surround' and 'MiniSurround' will mean the same thing.
- Each supplied config table is stored in config field of global object. Like MiniSurround.config.
- Values of config which affect runtime activity can be changed on the fly to have effect. For example, MiniSurround.config.n_lines can be changed during runtime; but changing MiniSurround.config.mappings won't have any effect (as mappings are created once during setup()).
- If module works best with some specific non-default option value, it is set during setup(). If the value is not essential to module's functionality, it is done only if user or another plugin hasn't set it beforehand (no matter the value).
Buffer local configuration #
Each module can be additionally configured to use certain runtime config settings locally to buffer. See mini.nvim-buffer-local-config section in help file for more information.
Buffer names #
All module-related buffers are named according to the following format: mini<module-name>://<buffer-number>/<useful-info> (forward slashes are used on any platform; <useful-info> may be empty). This structure allows creating identifiable, reasonably unique, and useful buffer names. For example, 'mini.files' buffers are created per displayed directory/file with names like minifiles://10/path/to/displayed/directory.
Disabling #
Each module's core functionality can be disabled globally or locally to buffer. See "Disabling" section in module's help page for more details. See mini.nvim-disabling-recipes section in main help file for common recipes.
Silencing #
Each module providing non-error feedback (like a reminder to press a key after some idle time in 'mini.ai', 'mini.jump2d', 'mini.surround') can be configured to not do that by setting config.silent = true (either inside setup() call or on the fly).
Highlighting #
Appearance of module's output is controlled by certain set of highlight groups (see :h highlight-groups). By default they usually link to some semantically close built-in highlight group and are ensured to be defined after any color scheme takes effect. Use :highlight command or vim.api.nvim_set_hl() Lua function to customize highlighting. To see a more calibrated look, use 'mini.hues', 'mini.base16', or plugin's color scheme.
Stability #
Each module upon release is considered to be relatively stable: both in terms of setup and functionality. Any non-bugfix backward-incompatible change will be released gradually as much as possible.
Not filetype and language specific #
Including functionality which needs several filetype/language specific implementations is an explicit no-goal of this project. This is mostly due to the potential increase in maintenance to keep implementation up to date. However, any part which might need filetype/language specific tuning should be designed to allow it by letting user set proper buffer options and/or local configuration.
Text edit repeat #
All text edit mappings (like for operators, textobjects, motions) created by modules support built-in repeat functionality if technically possible. This includes dot-repeat, macros, and Neovim>=0.13 multicursor.
Plugin color schemes #
This plugin comes with several color schemes (all have both dark and light variants). Activate any of them as a regular colorscheme (like :colorscheme minischeme or vim.cmd.colorscheme('minischeme')).
- Based on 'mini.hues' (recommended): 
  - minischeme: blue and yellow main color scheme.
  - miniwinter: "icy winter" palette with azure background.
  - minispring: "blooming spring" palette with green background.
  - minisummer: "hot summer" palette with brown/yellow background.
  - miniautumn: "cooling autumn" palette with purple background.
  - randomhue: random background and foreground of the same hue with medium saturation.
You can see how they look in 'mini.hues' README.
- Based on 'mini.base16': 
  - minicyan: cyan and grey main colors with medium contrast and saturation palette.
  - miniblue: blue and yellow main colors with high contrast and saturation palette.
You can see how they look in 'mini.base16' README.
Planned modules #
This is the list of modules I currently intend to implement eventually (as my free time and dedication will allow), in alphabetical order:
- 'mini.abbrev' - helper to manage/setup Insert mode abbreviations.
- 'mini.cycle' - cycle through alternatives with pre-defined rules. Something like monaqa/dial.nvim and AndrewRadev/switch.vim
- 'mini.folds' - more capable and user-friendly folds.
- 'mini.repl' - extendable wrapper for REPLs with built-in support for R, Python, Julia, and maybe (just maybe) some AI tools.
- 'mini.sendtext' - send text between buffers. In particular between regular and built-in terminal buffers.
- 'mini.terminals' - coherently manage interactive terminal buffers. Something like kassio/neoterm. Might also incorporate functionality to asynchronously run code in shell with post-processed results.
- 'mini.quickfix' - more capable and user-friendly quickfix list. Possibly with preview and inline editing for search-and-replace workflow.
- 'mini.windows' - window manager. Interactive picker, layout organizer, and maybe more.

Parcel: A desktop mail client for Linux, built with Zig
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-15
23:54:39 UTC
08:54:39 KST

- Zig 99%
- HTML <1%
- CSS <1%
- Python <1%
- Shell <1%
- 1 more language <1%
parcel #
A mail client for Gmail and Fastmail on the Linux desktop, built with Zig and siv.
Parcel shows mail as one list, chosen by label filters you stack: Inbox, or Inbox and Work, or any label alone. Every action has a key, and Ctrl+K lists them all. It reads your Gmail, Fastmail, or any JMAP server once you sign in, and shows sample mail until then. Each account has its own list, and the header switches between them.
A look around #
A thread opens over the list. Quoted replies nest, each level under a rule of its own, and HTML mail shows as its sender laid it out.
r replies, over a quote of what you answer. The editor has Vim's keys
and a toolbar for marks, links, quotes, and lists.
/ searches as you type, with Gmail's operators, whichever account it
is. Right after an operator such as from:, it suggests the people,
labels, or values it takes. Parcel keeps its own index of your mail, and
once it has been through all of it, answers most searches without asking
the server.
The mail in these screenshots is made up.
Build it #
Parcel needs Zig 0.17.1, just, a Wayland compositor, and the development files for libcurl, Wayland, xkbcommon, Fontconfig, and the Vulkan headers:
sudo apt install just libcurl4-openssl-dev libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev libfontconfig-dev libvulkan-dev  # Debian, Ubuntu
sudo dnf install just libcurl-devel wayland-devel libxkbcommon-devel fontconfig-devel vulkan-headers        # Fedora
sudo pacman -S just curl wayland libxkbcommon fontconfig vulkan-headers                                     # Arch
Then:
just run
Install it #
just install
This puts parcel in ~/.local/bin, and its desktop entry and icon in
~/.local/share, so app launchers list Parcel. Pass another prefix to
install elsewhere, such as just install /usr/local (with sudo).
Sign in #
Parcel opens on sample mail under its Add account page until it has an account; after that, the palette's Add account (Ctrl+K) opens the page. Sign in with Google, Fastmail, or another JMAP server; the account opens as soon as you have, named for the address you signed in with.
Each account has a name, its directory's under
~/.local/state/parcel/accounts, which the header shows and Ctrl+1 to
Ctrl+9 count in sorted order. Rename an account by renaming its directory
while parcel is not running.
Gmail #
Gmail signs in in the browser with Parcel's own Google client, which
release builds carry. An account's refresh token is kept in its
directory's google-token, readable only by you.
Where a Google Workspace admin blocks apps they have not approved, ask
them to trust Parcel's client ID. Or use a client of your own, which
Parcel prefers whenever it is there; a build from source without
-Dgoogle-client-secret needs one too:
- In the Google Cloud console, enable the Gmail API for a project: your organization's, where Workspace trusts its own apps.
- Under Google Auth Platform, create a client of type Desktop app. For a project outside your organization, add yourself as a test user.
- Download the client's JSON and save it as
~/.config/parcel/google-client.json.
- Add the account, and sign in in the browser it opens.
A sign-in works only with the client that made it, so an account signed
in with your own client keeps needing its file. While your project's app
is in testing, Google expires the sign-in after seven days; sign in again
then with parcel login gmail NAME.
Fastmail and other JMAP servers #
Fastmail signs in in the browser: Parcel registers itself with Fastmail
as it signs in, so there is nothing to set up. Another JMAP server does
the same where it offers OAuth for desktop apps; give it the server's
address. Either one also takes a token in place of the browser: for
Fastmail, make one in Settings, Privacy & Security, Manage API tokens,
with access to Email and Email submission; a token of the form
user:password goes as Basic authorization.
The sign-in is kept in the account's directory, readable only by you:
jmap-oauth for the browser's, jmap-token for a token. From a terminal,
parcel login fastmail NAME and
parcel login jmap NAME https://mail.example.org/.well-known/jmap sign in
with a token too.
Work on it #
mise installs the toolchain, including
bs, the Debug-mode compiler used for
development builds, which also lints: mise install, then just setup
for the baskingspot lint rules. just --list shows the recipes, and just ci builds
parcel and runs the tests and lint. AGENTS.md has the conventions.

Indian chip startup Bharat Semi lands $24M seed round as it eyes global AI sensor market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-15
23:30:00 UTC
08:30:00 KST

Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.
The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.
India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.
The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.
“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.
Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.
Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.
The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.
The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.
Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.
“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said.
In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.
The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

Pranksters Redirect Bitly's Links in X Posts for Trump, McDonald's and Burger King
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-15
23:13:00 UTC
08:13:00 KST

Pranksters Redirect Bitly's Links in X Posts for Trump, McDonald's and Burger King (kwwl.com) 20
			
		 	
				"A massive link-hijacking scheme has turned corporate social media archives into bizarre and offensive redirects," reports the New York Post:
Posts from high-profile accounts — including fast-food giants McDonald's and Burger King, as well as President Donald Trump — are getting hacked, with over decades-old links suddenly redirecting users to unrelated website links including links about 9/11 and the Holocaust.
An unknown party appears to be taking control of expired Bitly link shorteners — a widely used URL-shortening and link-management service — and altering their destinations....
Another Burger King tweet from July 13, 2011 — reading, "Now it's even easier to eat right at BURGER KING® restaurants with @WeRRestaurants. All you need is a zip code!" — was warped to link straight to Adolf Hitler's Wikipedia page... Two posts on Donald Trump's X account were also altered: a 2013 post redirected to a "Baby Fortnite" page, while a 2012 post linked to a video of Mario and Luigi from Super Mario Bros.
 
The article notes that about 20 of Trump's old X posts had "switched" links, including some now pointing to videos of the Transformers.  And it adds that "outraged web users are also slamming Bitly over its flaw that allows links to 'die' and be recycled by pranksters and bad actors."
"Links dating as far back as 2009 from URL-shortening service Bitly were affected," reports CNN, "and only corporate and political X accounts appear to have been targeted, with President Donald Trump's personal account seemingly hit the hardest."  "Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and former Vice President Mike Pence... were also hit to varying degrees."
Bitly said Sunday afternoon in a post on X that it had "identified an issue that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links to redirect people to content unrelated to the original posts." The company said it suspended the accounts that altered links and were working to disable the affected URLs...   It's unclear whether hackers made custom Bitly links, which effectively allow them to copy the original URL and redirect to any website. That may have been possible if the original Bitly link to the website no longer exists or has expired.... Another 2013 post from Trump tagged former Republican nominee for president Mitt Romney, and links to the popular game "Geometry Dash"....
A post in 2011 by Trudeau contains a Bitly link that redirects to a vulgar YouTube audio clip...   Government accounts have also been ironically affected. A 2012 post from the FBI about computers infected by "Ghost Clicks" now directs to a page with a photo of a seal, while the Department of Defense account had a separately redirected post.

Preserving 30 Years of Salon Journalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-15
23:00:11 UTC
08:00:11 KST

When Salon launched in 1995, the web was still finding its voice. One of the first major publications born on the internet, Salon helped define a new kind of digital journalism, bringing together politics, culture, criticism, and ideas for a generation of online readers.
After 31 years, Salon has announced that it is ceasing publication. But thanks to web archiving, the stories don’t have to disappear.
The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has been preserving Salon for nearly three decades—the online publication has been published over time at salon1999.com, salonmag.com and, since 1999, salon.com. Today, more than 250,000 Salon articles can be discovered through the Wayback Machine, representing a record of digital journalism and the conversations that shaped our culture since the earliest days of the web.
To make exploring this web archive easier, we’ve also launched an experimental Salon Explorer, a new interface for discovering Salon’s archived journalism. Browse more than 250,000 articles and explore the work of over 20,000 writers using filters that make it easier to find stories and discover writing you may have missed.
Explore the Salon archive:

Show HN: The Last Complication, a Zachtronics-style watchmaking puzzle game
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-15
22:48:52 UTC
07:48:52 KST

Thirty houses, counted down the first row, back up the second and down the third. The strip beside the board is the week: ten throws, taken in order, and then again from the top.
A throw moves one counter exactly that many houses. One counter to a house, and none may pass two that stand together.
Every counter stops on the 26th house. The 27th is water: a counter that lands there goes back to the 15th. A counter leaves the board by the exact count.
If a counter can move, one must. A throw that none can use is left over, and the game is lost.
The bench is laid out for a tall screen.

The Popular Cutting Board That Replaced My Old Plastic Ones Is on Early Sale for Black Friday
One of the quiet MVPs of my kitchen is the humble cutting board. They are so necessary for me that I have seven — in different shapes and sizes, no less. Most of them are plastic, though. In the last few months, I’ve been trying to move away from plastic in my kitchen due to the potentially hazardous effects microplastics could have on our bodies (shoutout to our Senior Lifestyle Editor Quinn Fish for putting me on to this).
Naturally, I’ve been looking for plastic-free alternatives, and while I love my paper composite Epicurean boards, I’ve also become a major fan of Material’s The MK Free Board. The plant-based cutting board is huge, making it perfect for meal prepping, family dinners, and big baking projects. I’ve only been using it for a couple weeks, but now I don’t want to be without it!
What You Should Know About Material’s The MK Free Board
Material is known for its stylish (and useful) kitchenware, like knives, cooking utensils, tableware, nonstick pans, and more. I’ve been a big fan of the brand’s reBoard, which is a beautiful BPA-free plastic- and sugarcane-based cutting board that has sold out 10 times (unsurprisingly, it’s currently out of stock).
For a completely plastic-free option, I turned to The MK Free Board, which Material introduced earlier this year. It’s made from “100% plant-based biocomposite of natural clay minerals and biodegradable biopolymers,” the brand says. Like my plastic cutting boards, this one is also dishwasher-safe, which gives it a major leg up for me over wooden versions.
This best-selling cutting board is 17.5 inches long (making it just a tab bit longer than the Wonder Oven Pro), comes in three colors, and is on sale for just $41 right now. It’s a real hit with customers, too, who’ve given it a collective 4.8-star rating.
My Honest Review of Material’s The MK Free Board
Because I love the reBoard, I had high hopes for The MK Free Board — and it did not disappoint. It’s roomy enough to work on two different recipes at once. I cut up broccoli on one half then used the other half to slice open a vanilla bean for Ina Garten’s Brownie Pudding right after.
The board has two different sides, too: one with a groove to catch runoff from tomatoes or meat, and one that’s completely flat. I usually prefer the flat side for cutting veggies and fruit, but I make roasted pork tenderloin once a week, and the other side is perfect for that.
So far, I’m impressed that there aren’t any knife scratch marks on the board yet, or any staining. It also fits in my dishwasher without issue, even though it’s quite large.
If you’re going plastic-free or stocking up on holiday gifts for the cooks in your life, look no further!
